title: Book 9 — Calliope, Chapter 120
paragraphs: Then, as the men of the Chersonese say, as one of those who guarded them was frying dried fish, a portent occurred as follows: the dried fish, when laid on the fire, began to leap and struggle as if they were fish newly caught. The others gathered round and marveled at the portent, but Artaÿctes, seeing it, called to the man frying the fish and said: “Stranger of Athens, be not at all afraid of this portent, since it has not appeared for you but for me. Protesilaos, who dwells at Elaius, is signifying by this that though he is dead and his body is dried like those fish, yet he has power given him by the gods to exact vengeance from the man who does him wrong. Now, therefore, I wish to impose this penalty for him: in place of the things I took from the temple, I will pay down a hundred talents to the god; and moreover, as ransom for myself and my son, I will pay two hundred talents to the Athenians, if my life be spared.” So he undertook, but he did not persuade the commander Xanthippos; for the people of Elaius, desiring to take vengeance for Protesilaos, asked that he be put to death, and the commander's own inclination tended to the same conclusion. They brought him, therefore, to that headland where Xerxes made his crossing — or, as some say, to the hill above the town of Madytos — and there they nailed him to boards and hung him up; and they stoned his son to death before the eyes of Artaÿctes himself.
